summary: Learners aged 7–9 come to know Mary Anning (1799–1847) of Lyme Regis as a self-taught, working-class fossil hunter who found important marine-reptile skeletons in the early 1800s, understand why those finds mattered as evidence for extinction, and grapple with the fact that she was often uncredited and barred from the scientific establishment as a poor woman. The lead approach is a story-and-perspective encounter in her voice; supporting approaches add a spatial/temporal anchor (cliff scene plus timeline), a re-enactment of fieldwork, and a light fact check. A recurring correction throughout: ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs are marine reptiles, not dinosaurs.
misconceptions: 'Mary Anning found dinosaurs' — her famous finds (ichthyosaur, plesiosaur) were marine reptiles, not dinosaurs.
'Fossil hunting was a safe hobby' — she worked dangerous, crumbling sea cliffs and sold fossils to survive.
'She was a trained, wealthy scientist' — she was a self-taught working-class woman, largely outside the formal scientific establishment.
'She was always famous and credited' — much of her work was published by men without acknowledging her; recognition came largely later.
'Her finds didn't change science' — they were crucial evidence that extinction was real.

activities.title: Meet Mary Anning in her own voice
steps: Picture standing on the windy shingle beach at Lyme Regis while Mary Anning works the cliffs, and ask her questions such as 'What did you find?', 'Was it dangerous?', and 'Why wasn't your name on the discoveries?'

Listen to her describe how her brother Joseph found a strange giant ichthyosaur skull (around 1811) and how she, as a girl of about 12, found and dug out the rest of the skeleton, and how she later uncovered the first nearly complete plesiosaur skeleton (1823)
Ask her why fossil hunting was risky and hear about working the crumbling sea cliffs and the landslides that endangered fossil hunters — one cliff-fall killed her dog Tray and nearly killed her

Ask her why her name was often missing from the discoveries and hear, plainly, that gentlemen bought her fossils and wrote scientific papers about them, often without naming her as the finder, and that as a woman she could not even join the Geological Society
Ask 'Were they dinosaurs?' and hear her correction that her famous beasts were sea reptiles, not dinosaurs
Retell, in your own words, one thing she found and one reason she matters
activities.insight: Mary Anning was a real person whose discoveries were key evidence that whole kinds of animals had gone extinct — a radical idea at the time — and whose lack of credit as a poor woman raises the question of who gets to do science and who gets remembered.

activities.title: Explore the Lyme Regis cliffs and a life timeline
steps: Tap features of a Lyme Regis cliff scene to reveal each labelled find — ichthyosaur and plesiosaur — and where along the coast she hunted
Tap points on a timeline of the early 1800s to reveal key life events and discoveries in order
Open a 'Why wasn't she credited?' panel to read, at an age-appropriate level, that her work was often published by men without naming her and that she could not join the Geological Society
Compare a 'credit then vs now' contrast: unnamed in old papers → celebrated today
Compare a 'before/after' on the idea of extinction to see what her fossils helped prove
activities.insight: The who/what/where of Anning's life — Lyme Regis, early 1800s, fossils in the sea cliffs — together with why her finds mattered and why she was overlooked.

activities.title: Prospect the Jurassic Coast like Anning
steps: Prospect a cliff scene safely to search for fossils where Anning worked
Uncover an ichthyosaur or plesiosaur specimen
Log and label the find as Anning did, noting that it is a marine reptile
Discuss what makes this hunting dangerous (crumbling cliffs, landslides)
activities.insight: A felt sense of what Anning actually did in the field — careful searching, uncovering, and identifying specimens — and that this was hazardous, hands-on work.

activities.title: Check the key facts and the big 'why'
steps: Match each find to its name (ichthyosaur, plesiosaur)
Answer why her work mattered and why she was often overlooked

Respond to the diagnostic prompt: 'Mary Anning dug up the skeleton of an ichthyosaur — a giant sea creature no one had ever seen alive. Why was a discovery like this so important for science? And does finding it make Mary Anning a dinosaur hunter?'
Explain in your own words whether ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs were dinosaurs
activities.insight: Secure recall of place, era, a named find, and the significance (evidence for extinction and prehistoric life), while distinguishing marine reptiles from dinosaurs.

checkQuestion: Mary Anning dug up the skeleton of an ichthyosaur — a giant sea creature no one had ever seen alive. Why was a discovery like this so important for science? And does finding it make Mary Anning a dinosaur hunter?
checkAnswer: Her fossils were evidence that creatures once lived that no longer exist anywhere — helping people accept that species can go extinct and that prehistoric life was different from today. But ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs were marine reptiles, not dinosaurs, so she was a fossil hunter rather than strictly a dinosaur hunter.
